I want to address this issue as best as I can, but I can only speak from my own experience. So, here we go. I have never had a trans- friend in my life. It's not that I have chosen to not have a trans- friend. The opportunity has simply never presented itself. I had an intersex friend in college. A casual friend, but a friend, nonetheless. That's probably the closest I've known someone to be experiencing the issue that you are having. But, since you originally framed it as a blanket question for broaching controversial topics, I will speak to that.

My sister came out of the closet when she entered college. I had suspected for years, but since it was none of my business, and she never wanted to talk about it, I just treated her as my sister. Interestingly enough, I was one of the last of my family members to "officially" be told. She approached my parents first, and even though I wasn't there to witness the discussion, it was reportedly a disaster. You see, my parents are faux-liberals. They call themselves Democrats, but cast votes for pieces of shit like Ross Perot and George W. Bush. They are walking contradictions. They put on airs about being open-minded, non-judgmental persons, when they are anything but. And this was sort of the inherent problem about this. My sister thought she could approach them, because they claim to be so accepting, only to discover that this was most certainly not the case.

After all of this happened, and I finally got wind of it, my mother brought the subject up with me. She... just... doesn't... get it. I swear. Trying to explain homosexuality to my mother is like trying to explain space travel to my cat. You might as well be talking to a brick wall. You know, it sucks. It does. My sister moved halfway across the country to start a new life, and has purposefully cut off contact with them, and I don't blame her one bit. They have been awful to her. My mother does this thing that I call "resentment gifts," where she will buy you presents in order to express her disdain about something. When my sister gave away all of her dresses because she had no desire to wear them, my mother bought her new ones. She does this with me, too, and it is one of the worst qualities about her. Both of us have had to undergo significant amounts of therapy because of the abusive way she has treated us, and I've had therapists tell me that it's healthy to create boundaries, and have limited contact with them, because of these issues.

Now, I know this was long-winded and depressing. But I'm getting to my point. You see, some people you can't change. You can't make them understand. Sometimes you have a cat, and no matter how well you can dissect theoretical physics and the wonders of the universe, your cat still won't understand how SpaceX is trying to colonize Mars. That's just the way it is, sometimes, and there's nothing you can do about it. Some people (and cats) are ignorant. It's not their choice. It's no more their choice to be ignorant than it is your choice to be transgendered, than it is a choice for my sister to be gay, than it is a choice for my cat to be fucking retarded. And once you can accept that, then you can finally make peace with yourself and the world.

My relationship with my parents is strained. There's no question about that. And, on paper, there could be a lot of regrets about not having the picture-perfect depiction of a family that sitcoms shove down our throats. But I can't regret it, because it wasn't my choice. My parents were the ones who decided to not accept my "flaws" (their interpretation), or my sister's "flaws" (also, their interpretation).

So, here is my advice: be honest; be courageous; be brave; be strong; be bold; and most importantly, be yourself. It's obviously important to you that your mother understand, and it's worth trying to make that happen. But sit down with her, explain the situation, explain that who you are is not a choice, and express your desire to understood, accepted, and loved. If she is resistant, then that is her choice, and her choice alone. You have done everything in your power. And, at that point, the only thing that you have the power to do is the exact thing that you desire from your mother: accept it. She may be unwilling to accept you as a person, despite all of your "flaws" (her interpretation), which makes it all the more important for you to accept her "flaws" (your/my interpretation). Be the bigger person. Search for those who support you. Surround yourself with those who support you. Create your own network of loving, caring, understanding people, and live in that world. And remember that The Dinner Table has your back.
